title: SRE standards: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, and runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Summary
=======
This document defines Redwood Inference's SRE standards for Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical runbook structure. It is intended as a reference for service owners, on-call engineers, and product teams to ensure consistent reliability practices across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Scope
-----
Applies to all externally visible production services owned by Redwood Inference (control plane, public API, inference runtime, model store, console). Internal tooling and non-production environments SHOULD follow the same templates but MAY use more relaxed thresholds.

1) SLO and error budget definitions
----------------------------------
Intro: An SLO is a target level of service (availability or latency) that a service must meet. Error budgets are the allowable amount of unreliability over a rolling time window.

Key service categories and baseline SLOs (examples; teams must adopt or justify deviations):
- Control plane API (authentication, routing, config): Availability 99.95% monthly; latency P95 < 150ms, P99 < 500ms.
- Public Text Generation API: Availability 99.90% monthly; latency P95 < 250ms, P99 < 800ms.
- Inference runtime (per-request model exec): Availability 99.8% monthly; tail latency P99 < 1s for standard models (smaller models may have lower targets).
- Embeddings API: Availability 99.9% monthly; P95 < 200ms.
- Console and dashboards: Availability 99.5% monthly; P95 < 300ms.

Measurements and windows:
- Primary window: 30-day rolling window for availability/error budget.
- Secondary window: 7-day for operational alerts and burn-rate detection.
- Aggregation: Measure errors by request class (successful vs. failed HTTP 5xx, timeout, degraded response). Latency SLOs are computed using request latency distributions with service-level filters (exclude maintenance, feature-flagged changes when annotated).

SLO ownership and metadata (required per SLO):
- service_name (string)
- primary_owner (pager rota / team)
- SLO_type (availability | latency | correctness)
- target (e.g., 99.9%)
- measurement_window (30d)
- alert_thresholds (see Operational tooling)
- related_runbook (confluence link)

2) Error budget policy and escalation
------------------------------------
Policy summary:
- Error budget = 1 - SLO. Teams may consume error budget for scheduled releases, capacity changes, or controlled experiments.
- Burn-rate detection: Continuous monitoring computes the burn rate against the 30d budget.

Escalation rules (examples):
1. Burn rate > 2x sustained for 1 hour: Notify on-call and SLO owner (PagerDuty).
2. Burn rate > 4x sustained for 30 minutes: Page on-call (P1) and notify engineering manager + product manager; open an incident ticket.
3. Remaining error budget < 20% (rolling 7-day): Weekly review with reliability lead; consider release freeze for feature rollouts.
4. Error budget exhausted: Mandatory incident review and rollback of highest-risk changes in the last 14 days; require approval for further rollouts until budget is replenished.

Communication and reporting:
- Slack channel: #sre-burn-alerts (aggregated).
- Weekly reliability digest sent to eng-leads with per-service burn rates and corrective actions.

3) Capacity planning and forecasting
------------------------------------
Objectives: Ensure capacity to meet both latency and throughput SLOs while optimizing cost.

Planning cadence and owners:
- Quarterly capacity review owned by Platform SRE (capacity-planning@redwood.ai) with input from product usage forecasts and sales pipeline for Dedicated/Private high-commit customers.
- Monthly operational health check for headroom metrics.

Key metrics and thresholds:
- Target headroom: 30% nominal free capacity on critical resources (GPU vRAM, GPU SM utilization, inference worker threads) during expected peak traffic.
- Autoscaling trigger (horizontal): average utilization >= 70% for 5 minutes triggers scale out; scale in at utilization <= 45% for 10 minutes.
- Queue depth threshold: request queue > 200ms * average processing_time triggers investigation and scale actions.
- Cold-start budget: maintain at least one warm replica per model variant in each active region for low-latency customers.

Forecasting model:
- Inputs: 90-day usage trend, customer commit changes (Dedicated/Private), marketing events, model size/seq-length distribution, per-model token rates.
- Outputs: capacity plan (instances, GPU types, regional placement), cost estimate, rollout schedule.

Capacity testing and validation:
- Run synthetic load tests quarterly (benchmarks in eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite).
- Validate autoscaler behaviour in staging with 1.5x expected peak load before production changes.

4) Reliability initiatives and OKRs
----------------------------------
Program structure:
- Initiative owners define clear success metrics (reduction in P99 latency, increase in availability, error budget savings).
- Typical initiatives: intelligent batching, KV-cache hit-rate improvement, model quantization profiles, autoscaler improvements, fallback routing.

Example OKR:
- O: Reduce 99th percentile inference latency by 20% for medium models in EU region by end of Q3.
- KR1: Deploy continuous batching improvements to runtime (5% median throughput improvement).
- KR2: Increase prefix cache hit rate from 45% to 65% for top-20 customer prompts.

Investment and prioritization:
- Use error-budget-weighted ROI: initiatives that save >0.5% monthly error budget per $k invested get priority.

5) Incident review standards
---------------------------
Post-incident expectations:
- Postmortem owner: incident commander (IC) or on-call lead.
- Deadline: Draft postmortem within 72 hours; final postmortem within 14 days.
- Required sections: Summary, Impact, Timeline, Root cause, Contributing factors, Corrective actions, Preventative actions with owners and due dates, Metrics for verification.

Severity classification and sampling for reviews:
- Sev 1: total outage or major degradation affecting >50% customer traffic or critical workloads. All Sev 1 postmortems require executive review.
- Sev 2: partial outage with significant customer impact. Requires peer review.
- Sev 3: minor impact or localized degradation; team review.

Blameless culture and remediation tracking:
- Focus on systems and process fixes. Track follow-up tasks in JIRA with the label "postmortem-action" and link them in the postmortem.
- Quarterly reliability review meeting to surface recurring themes.

6) Operational tooling and dashboards
------------------------------------
Required dashboards (per service):
- SLO dashboard: current SLI, rolling 30d SLO status, burn rate visualization.
- Capacity dashboard: GPU/CPU utilization, queue depth, per-replica memory and vRAM, autoscaler status.
- Error-classification dashboard: top error types by count and percent, latency distributions by request class.
- Customer-impact correlation: map of customer IDs to error rates (for Dedicated/Private customers with consent).

Alerting policy (examples):
- SLO alert: SLO error budget burn rate > 2x for 1 hour => P2 alert to SRE channel.
- Latency alert: P99 latency > SLO target + 30% for 15 minutes => P2.
- Capacity alert: GPU vRAM utilization > 85% or OOM errors observed => P1 page to on-call.

Tooling recommendations:
- Metrics: Prometheus + Thanos for long-term retention.
- Tracing: Jaeger with request sampling at 1% baseline and increased sampling during incidents.
- Dashboards: Grafana with standardized folders per service.
- Burn-rate: a dedicated service that computes burn rate per SLO and writes to the SLO dashboard and PagerDuty.

7) SRE runbooks (canonical template)
-----------------------------------
All runbooks MUST follow this template and live in confluence under eng-sre/runbooks with a single-line summary in the page title.

Runbook template (use copy-paste):
- Title: <service> - <short summary>
- Owned by: <team> (pager rota)
- Pager: <PagerDuty escalation>
- Severity: <expected severity on-call should expect>
- Symptoms: bullet list of typical symptoms (metrics/alerts)
- Immediate actions (ordered):
  1. Acknowledge pager and claim incident in tracker.
  2. Verify scope: run `curl -s -I https://<service>/health` and check response codes and latency.
  3. If 5xx spike or >X% error, set an emergency rollback flag via `kubectl annotate deployment <svc> emergency-rollback=true` (internal tooling).
  4. If GPU OOMs: run `kubectl logs <pod> | grep OOM` and scale down model concurrency by setting `model.concurrency` in the runtime config to 1.
  5. If queue depth high: add worker replicas: `./infra/scale.sh --service <svc> --replicas +2` and monitor queue.
  6. If degraded responses only for large-seq requests: enable fallback routing to compact model: `route-policy set <svc> fallback-compact true`
- Diagnostic commands (copy/paste):
  - `kubectl get pods -l app=<svc> -o wide`
  - `promql avg_over_time(http_request_duration_seconds[5m])`
  - `promql sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[1m])) by (instance)`
- Communication checklist:
  - Post an update every 15 minutes in the incident Slack thread.
  - Update statuspage if customer-visible outage (use templates).
- Post-incident tasks:
  - Capture timeline and tag metrics.
  - Create postmortem draft within 72 hours.
  - Schedule follow-up work and add to backlog with due dates.

8) Review and governance
------------------------
- SLO and runbook review cadence: annual SLA/SLO review for each service, with major review after any Sev 1 or two Sev 2 incidents.
- Documentation ownership: service owners must keep runbooks and SLO metadata up-to-date; SRE guild performs quarterly audits.
- Exceptions: Any deviation from these standards requires a documented exception request reviewed by the reliability lead and the head of engineering.

Appendix A — Example SLO metadata table
--------------------------------------
| service_name | primary_owner | SLO_type | target | measurement_window | alert_thresholds | related_runbook |
|--------------|---------------|----------|--------|--------------------|------------------|-----------------|
| public-api   | api-team      | availability | 99.9% | 30d | burn_rate>2x(1h) | /eng-sre/runbooks/public-api-health |
| inference-runtime | runtime-sre | latency (P99) | 1s | 30d | p99>1.3s(15m) | /eng-sre/runbooks/inference-runtime-high-latency |

Appendix B — Quick links and references
---------------------------------------
- Benchmarking suite: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite
- Capacity playbook: confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning
- Incident process and postmortem template: confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortem-template

Questions or exceptions should be directed to the reliability lead (reliability@redwood.ai) or raised in the SRE guild meetings.
